set.story: British historian C. Northcote Parkinson began a humorous 1955 essay in The Economist by calling it “a commonplace observation that work expands so as to fill the time available for its completion.”

why: Misquote: the essay's first sentence is 'It is a commonplace observation that work expands so as to fill the time available for its completion,' not the bare law as an opening line.

set.story: In the early second century AD, the Roman satirist Juvenal complained that the people, who once handed out power and armies, now longed for only two things: “bread and circuses,” meaning free grain and public games.

why: Satire 10 is in Juvenal's Book IV, generally dated to the 120s; 'around AD 100' is too early. 'Early second century AD' is safe.

ex: Fans showed pure doublethink, insisting the referee was both hopelessly incompetent and cleverly rigging the game.
Years of propaganda trained citizens in doublethink, so they believed the enemy was both pathetically weak and a terrifying threat.

why: Old ex 1 showed hypocrisy and ex 2 (calling pay cuts a 'compensation enhancement') showed doublespeak/euphemism, a classic confusion; neither showed holding two contradictory beliefs at once.

ex: Stuck in traffic, Diego became a Walter Mitty, imagining himself as a race-car champion.
During long bus rides, Priya turned into a Walter Mitty, picturing herself leading daring mountain rescues.

why: Ex 2 (an executive who invented his military record) shows the British 'fantasist/liar' usage, not the daydreaming sense the def teaches.

ex: After one weekend golf lesson, Liam started correcting the club pro's swing—the Dunning-Kruger effect in action.
The Dunning-Kruger effect may explain why beginner chess players feel sure they can beat experts.

why: Ex 1 (layman lecturing doctors about vaccines) touches a politically charged topic; spec requires neutral content.
A 'Walter Mitty' fantasizing about being better than the CEO could plausibly be picked for the cloze about a rookie sure he could run the company.
Jonah (a person who brings bad luck to those around them) overlaps with 'a person who spreads ... some harmful influence'; ambiguous for the definition questions.

cloze.s: “You have hissed all my mystery lectures” is a famous ___ attributed to an Oxford don.

why: Spooner was a fellow/lecturer and Warden of New College, not a professor; 'Oxford don' is accurate.

ex: Staff still call the year of layoffs and frozen pay the winter of our discontent.
Fans called the team's long losing streak the winter of our discontent.

why: Ex 1 'the company's winter of our discontent' had a clashing possessive (company's ... our).

ex: Tired of the neighbors' endless fence fight, Hannah said, “A plague on both your houses.”
Asked to pick a side in the feud between the two unions, the editor wrote simply, “A plague on both your houses.”

why: Ex 2 'took a plague on both your houses view' was ungrammatical without hyphenation/quotation.

ex: When auditors found missing invoices and shredded files, one muttered, “Something is rotten in the state of Denmark.”
Three managers quit in one week, and staff whispered that something is rotten in the state of Denmark.

why: Ex 1 had a tense clash ('it was clear something is rotten'); recast as a quotation.

cloze.s: The financial adviser was drowning in credit card debt, so when he lectured clients about saving, one replied, “___.”

why: Old cloze 'invited a quick physician, heal thyself from his clients' was awkward to fill grammatically.
'false memory' is an individual phenomenon, not a synonym for a shared collective false memory.
'observer effect' is chiefly a physics term with a different meaning; not a genuine synonym.
'spoilsport' means someone who spoils others' fun, not someone who withholds what they cannot use; not a true synonym.
'mascot' today mainly means a team emblem/costumed character; its old 'lucky charm' sense is obscure and misleading as an antonym.
